facts.statement: Thomas Carr reassigned specimen FMNH PR308 to Daspletosaurus torosus in 1999 after discovering that many skull features were plaster models.

facts.statement: In 2024, Warshaw and colleagues suggested that Dinosaur Park specimens likely belong to Daspletosaurus wilsoni.
facts.quote: In 2024, Warshaw and colleagues suggested that the Dinosaur Park specimens likely belong to D. wilsoni.

facts.statement: A tyrannosaurid specimen from New Mexico reported in 1990 was initially assigned to the genus Aublysodon.
facts.quote: A new tyrannosaurid specimen (OMNH 10131), including skull fragments, ribs, and parts of the hindlimb, was reported from New Mexico in 1990 and assigned to the now-defunct genus Aublysodon.

facts.statement: Research in 2010 reclassified a New Mexico tyrannosaurid specimen as a primitive tyrannosauroid in the genus Bistahieversor.
facts.quote: However, research published in 2010 showed that this species, from the Hunter Wash Member of the Kirtland Formation, is actually a more primitive tyrannosauroid, and was classified in the genus Bistahieversor.

facts.statement: Jack Horner and colleagues published a preliminary report in 1992 of a tyrannosaurid from the Two Medicine Formation in Montana.
facts.quote: In 1992, Jack Horner and colleagues published an extremely preliminary report of a tyrannosaurid from the upper parts of the Campanian Two Medicine Formation in Montana

facts.statement: The tyrannosaurid taxon from the Two Medicine Formation was named Daspletosaurus horneri in 2017.
facts.quote: In 2017, the Two Medicine Formation taxon was named as the new species D. horneri.

facts.statement: A Daspletosaurus specimen measuring approximately 11 meters long was reported from the Coal Ridge Member of the Judith River Formation in 2009.
facts.quote: In 2009, preliminary preparation of a Daspletosaurus specimen from the Coal Ridge Member of the Judith River Formation measuring about 11 m long was reported.

facts.statement: Ethan Warner-Cowgill and colleagues formally described a Daspletosaurus specimen in 2025, supporting the view that it is a distinct species.
facts.quote: In 2025, formal description of the specimen led by Ethan Warner-Cowgill concurred with the latter opinion.

facts.statement: A specimen known as "Sir William" was excavated between 2002 and 2004 and shows characteristics suggesting a new earlier species of Daspletosaurus.
facts.quote: A specimen in the collections of Triebold Paleontology excavated between 2002 and 2004, known as "Sir William" (RMDRC 2002.MT-001), shows some characteristics of Daspletosaurus suggesting a new earlier species to the genus.

facts.statement: Elías A. Warshaw and Denver W. Fowler described remains BDM 107 as the new species Daspletosaurus wilsoni in 2022.
facts.quote: Elías A. Warshaw and Denver W. Fowler described these remains (BDM 107) in 2022 as belonging to a new species of Daspletosaurus, D. wilsoni.

facts.statement: Daspletosaurus wilsoni is considered a transitional species existing between D. torosus and D. horneri in time.
facts.quote: It represents a transitional species between D. torosus and D. horneri, as it existed between them in time.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Daspletosaurus species evolved through anagenesis or if D. wilsoni is a junior synonym of D. torosus.
facts.quote: It has been suggested that the three species may have evolved directly through anagenesis, but this theory was disputed by Scherer and Voiculescu-Holvad (2024) who suggested that D. wilsoni may be a junior synonym of D. torosus

facts.statement: In 2025, researchers suggested that new features found in specimen CMC VP 15826 weaken the hypothesis that D. wilsoni and D. torosus are distinct species.
facts.quote: In 2025, Warner-Cowgill and colleagues described the largest known specimen of Daspletosaurus, CMC VP 15826 (nicknamed "Pete III"), identifying new anatomical features previously unknown from this genus and interpreting these characters as weakening the hypothesis that D. wilsoni and D. torosus are distinct species.

facts.statement: Adult Daspletosaurus could reach lengths of 8.5 to 9 meters, a hip height of 2.2 meters, and a mass of 2 to 3 metric tons.
facts.quote: Adults could reach a length of 8.5 - 9 m from snout to tail, a hip height of 2.2 m, and a body mass of 2 - 3 MT.

facts.statement: One large specimen suggests Daspletosaurus could reach lengths over 9 meters and weights of 4 to 5 metric tons.
facts.quote: However, one large specimen of Daspletosaurus sp. (CMC VP 15826) suggests that the genus could reach lengths of over 9 m, potentially reaching sizes of 11 m in length and 4 - 5 MT in weight.

facts.statement: Daspletosaurus had a massive skull reaching more than 1 meter in length.
facts.quote: Daspletosaurus had a massive skull that could reach more than 1 m in length.

facts.statement: The teeth in the premaxilla of Daspletosaurus had a D-shaped cross-section, an example of heterodonty common in tyrannosaurids.
facts.quote: Unlike its other teeth, those in the premaxilla at the end of the upper jaw had a D-shaped cross section, an example of heterodonty always seen in tyrannosaurids.

facts.statement: Split carinae have been found on the teeth of Daspletosaurus.
facts.quote: Split carinae (edges) have been found on Daspletosaurus teeth.

facts.statement: Daspletosaurus walked on two thick hindlimbs ending in four-toed feet, with the first digit not contacting the ground.
facts.quote: It walked on its two thick hindlimbs, which ended in four-toed feet, although the first digit (the hallux) did not contact the ground.

facts.statement: Daspletosaurus had extremely small forelimbs with only two digits, but possessed the longest forelimbs relative to body size of any tyrannosaurid.
facts.quote: In contrast, the forelimbs were extremely small and bore only two digits, although Daspletosaurus had the longest forelimbs in proportion to body size of any tyrannosaurid.

facts.statement: Comparisons of tooth wear suggest Daspletosaurus had lips that protected its teeth from external influences.
facts.quote: From a comparison of the degree of wear of teeth of Daspletosaurus with other extinct and extant animals, it is concluded that Daspletosaurus, as well as other non-avian theropods, had lips that protected the teeth from external influences.

facts.statement: Daspletosaurus is classified in the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae within the family Tyrannosauridae.
facts.quote: Daspletosaurus belongs in the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae within the family Tyrannosauridae, along with Tarbosaurus, Tyrannosaurus, and Alioramini.

facts.statement: Daspletosaurus belongs to the tribe Daspletosaurini, which also includes the taxon Thanatotheristes.
facts.quote: It further belongs to the tribe Daspletosaurini, consisting of it and the taxon Thanatotheristes.

facts.statement: Gregory Paul proposed reassigning Daspletosaurus torosus to the genus Tyrannosaurus, but this classification is not generally accepted.
facts.quote: Gregory Paul reassigned D. torosus to the genus Tyrannosaurus, creating the new combination Tyrannosaurus torosus, but this has not been generally accepted.

facts.statement: Some researchers suggest that Tarbosaurus and Tyrannosaurus are sister taxa or the same genus, with Daspletosaurus as a more basal relative.
facts.quote: Many researchers believe Tarbosaurus and Tyrannosaurus to be sister taxa or even to be the same genus, with Daspletosaurus a more basal relative.

facts.statement: Phil Currie and colleagues argue that Daspletosaurus is more closely related to Tarbosaurus and Asian tyrannosaurids like Alioramus than to North American Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: On the other hand, Phil Currie and colleagues find Daspletosaurus to be more closely related to Tarbosaurus and other Asian tyrannosaurids like Alioramus than to the North American Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: Scherer and Voiculescu-Holvad (2024) argued that overlapping stratigraphic ranges suggest Daspletosaurus species were contemporaneous and that anagenesis may not be the main driver of speciation.
facts.quote: In 2024, Scherer and Voiculescu-Holvad argued that the stratigraphic ranges of D. torosus, D. wilsoni and an unnamed species from the Dinosaur Park Formation and Oldman Formation show a clear overlap, indicating that anagenesis may not be the predominant factor of speciation within the genus, since all species of Daspletosaurus were contemporaneous with each other at some point during its evolution.

facts.statement: Scherer and Voiculescu-Holvad suggested that Daspletosaurus wilsoni might be a junior synonym of Daspletosaurus torosus due to a lack of distinguishing characters.
facts.quote: They also suggested that D. wilsoni may be a junior synonym of D. torosus, since there is a near lack of autapomorphic characters that can differentiate this species.

facts.statement: Warshaw and colleagues (2024) supported the anagenesis theory by validating D. wilsoni as a distinct taxon and reanalyzing previous studies.
facts.quote: In the same year, Warshaw and colleagues supported the anagenesis theory by referring other specimens to D. wilsoni (including the Dinosaur Park specimen) which they considered as a valid taxon, and by reanalysing the previous study of Scherer and Voiculescu-Holvad (2024).

facts.statement: Warshaw and colleagues proposed that Daspletosaurus is a paraphyletic genus ancestral to Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: They also recovered the paraphyletic Daspletosaurus at the base of Tyrannosaurini, making the genus ancestral to Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: Daspletosaurus horneri likely possessed integumentary sensory organs used for touch, jaw movement modulation, temperature sensing, and prey detection.
facts.quote: There are indications of D. horneri possessing integumentary sensory organs, possibly used in touch, modulation of precise jaw movements, temperature reading, and prey detection.

facts.statement: Large flat scales on Daspletosaurus may have protected its snout during prey capture and fights with other individuals.
facts.quote: The large flat scales may have further protected the snout during prey capture and intra-specific combat.

facts.statement: A full-grown Daspletosaurus from the Dinosaur Park Formation has tyrannosaur bite marks on its skull.
facts.quote: A full-grown Dinosaur Park Daspletosaurus (TMP 85.62.1) exhibits tyrannosaur bite marks on its skull.

facts.statement: Darren Tanke and Phil Currie hypothesize that bite marks on Daspletosaurus skulls resulted from intraspecific competition for territory, resources, or social dominance.
facts.quote: Darren Tanke and Phil Currie hypothesize that the bites are due to intraspecific competition for territory or resources, or for dominance within a social group.

facts.statement: A Daspletosaurus bonebed in Montana contains remains of three individuals: a large adult, a small juvenile, and an intermediate-sized individual.
facts.quote: The bonebed includes the remains of three Daspletosaurus, including a large adult, a small juvenile, and another individual of intermediate size.

facts.statement: Phil Currie speculates that Daspletosaurus formed packs, though this remains uncertain.
facts.quote: Currie speculates that the daspletosaurs formed a pack, although this cannot be stated with certainty.

facts.statement: Brian Roach and Daniel Brinkman suggest Daspletosaurus social interactions resembled modern Komodo dragons, involving non-cooperative mobbing and cannibalism, rather than cooperative packs.
facts.quote: Other scientists are skeptical of the evidence for social groups in Daspletosaurus and other large theropods; Brian Roach and Daniel Brinkman have suggested that Daspletosaurus social interaction would have more closely resembled the modern Komodo dragon, where non-cooperative individuals mob carcasses, frequently attacking and even cannibalizing each other in the process.

facts.statement: Evidence of cannibalism in Daspletosaurus was published in 2015.
facts.quote: Evidence of cannibalism in Daspletosaurus was published in 2015.

facts.statement: Daspletosaurus underwent a period of tremendous growth lasting about four years midway through its life.
facts.quote: Erickson has shown that after a long time as juveniles, tyrannosaurs underwent tremendous growth spurts for about four years midway through their lives.

facts.statement: The maximum growth rate of Daspletosaurus was 180 kilograms per year, based on an adult mass estimate of 1800 kg.
facts.quote: The maximum growth rate in Daspletosaurus was 180 kilograms (400 lb) per year, based on a mass estimate of 1800 kg in adults.

facts.statement: All known Daspletosaurus fossils date to the middle to late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, between 78 and 74.4 million years ago.
